about: The non-numeric claims of [JEngine], one record each: id, statement (in our vocabulary), source, kind, status, and either test (ASSERTED) or reason (PENDING / UNVERIFIABLE). See felizjueves.literature.claims. Ordered by id: add a record in its place rather than rewriting the file.

claims.statement: Alg. 1 line 10 writes J_p to global memory without atomics; once a class is split into batches, several kernels contribute to the same J_p, so the write needs atomics -- as §5 itself corrects.

The batch count is always a multiple of three: each of the x, y, z directions is split into the same number of sub-batches, and finer splits that break the three-way symmetry are both unnecessary and worse.
claims.reason: partition and Spec refuse any other count since #6 (test/test_plan_batching.py::test_an_illegal_batch_count_raises), but no test carries the claim mark yet, and test_plan_batching.py was outside #10's lane. The 'finer splits are worse' half is the paper's measurement.

claims.statement: A target's batch direction is the axis of its largest component, a tie going to the cyclic predecessor: {x,y} -> x, {y,z} -> y, {x,z} -> z, and all three equal -> x. This is deliberately the opposite convention to MILD's.
Raising the batch count lowers intermediates and targets per batch and raises total FLOPs across batches, because intermediates shared between batches are recomputed.
claims.reason: Post-sieve (#12) it holds at most cells but not at all of them. FLOPs are flat 1->3 at L = 7 (425, 425, where the paper prints 424, 425), and max intermediates per batch are flat 6->9 at L = 10 (95, 95). test/test_plan_sieve.py::test_batching_post_sieve pins both exceptions and carries no mark. At L = 7 the 1-batch sieve leaves one FLOP more than the paper's; a seed-order search (#13/#14) may close it.

claims.statement: eq. 17 prints the unit vector 1y as (1,1,0); it is (0,1,0). (1,1,0) is not a unit vector and would break eq. 11.
claims.reason: #8 records it in the docs; no code transcribes eq. 17 yet, so no test can hold the generator to (0,1,0).

claims.statement: The MILD tree obeys Johnson, Gill & Pople's optimal-tree rules 1, 2, 3 and 5: axial integrals {0 0 j} always present; reduce the unit component of {0 1 j}; never reduce the j of {1 1 j}; reduce the 2 of {0 2 j}.

MILD reduces along the smallest non-zero component of r (zeros excluded from the minimum) and breaks a tie toward the cyclic successor: rx=ry<rz -> y, ry=rz<rx -> z, rx=rz<ry -> x, and all three equal -> z.
Against Johnson et al.'s near-optimal tree search, MILD costs 1-2% more FLOPs and has 2-6% fewer intermediates.
claims.reason: Needs an exact (near-optimal) tree search to compare against, which this repo does not have.

claims.statement: For L <= 16, at most 9 batches are needed; the batch counts worth generating over are 1, 3, 6 and 9.
claims.reason: Not decidable by #13's cut search. Whether 9 batches suffice is relative to a register and shared-memory budget, and the plan layer models neither: PlanCost has no budget for max intermediates or max targets to fall under, so nothing in it marks a batch count as enough. It needs the kernel tier's measured spills and occupancy at 9 against 12 or more batches, once a generator emits kernels.

claims.statement: MILD cannot obey rule 4 (reduce to a parent and grandparent already in the tree): that is a property of the graph built so far, while MILD is a pure function of r. The sieve is the pass that recovers it.
The sieve's effect on register spills is non-monotone across classes: about 4% fewer on average, but [5|6] gets 3% more and [8|8] 11% fewer.
claims.reason: A spill count is a measurement of the paper's kernels on their compiler and their card (an A100), not a property of the tree -- the same argument that keeps Table 4 out of data/. The kernel tier can measure our own spills on sm_86 and gfx1200, but that is a different claim.

claims.statement: theta appears in eq. 13 (the fundamental) and is never defined; the conventional McMurchie-Davidson reading is theta^2 = zeta*eta/(zeta+eta), to be pinned against McMurchie & Davidson directly.

At L = 5 the batch Y_{1,2} (direction y, 1 <= ry <= 2) is exactly the eight targets { p_y, d_yz, d_y2, f_xy2, f_y2z, g_xy2z, g_y2z2, h_xy2z2 }; d_yz, g_y2z2 and h_xy2z2 are members only because of the tie-break.
claims.reason: Held by test/test_plan_batching.py::test_the_y_1_2_batch_is_the_papers_eight_targets since #6, but that test does not carry the claim mark yet, and test_plan_batching.py was outside #10's lane.
